title: Social Media, Misinformation, and Online Patient Education in Emergency General Surgical Procedures
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 200 most-viewed YouTube videos found with appendicitis and cholecystitis search terms. Alongside the DISCERN and PEMAT quality instruments, four surgical trainees rated each video on a dedicated 1-to-5 misinformation scale, and the paper reports shares of videos containing misinformation with a denominator (35% of 200 videos; 13.5% with more significant misinformation). That is explicit false-content coding by clinician reviewers, so it is CONTENT; the DISCERN and PEMAT scores are QUALITY and were not extracted.

estimates.country: Not stated; YouTube searched in English with no geographic restriction (the authors are US-based and describe the two procedures as the most common emergency general surgery procedures in the United States)
estimates.date: Search date not reported; videos had a median publication year of 2016 (Q1 2013, Q3 2018); instrument websites were accessed 9 August 2022 and the article was received 1 September 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of most-viewed YouTube videos on appendectomy and cholecystectomy rated as containing any misinformation
estimates.value_raw: More than a third (35%) of videos contained misinformation; Sixty five percent of videos did not contain misin- formation (Table 2: no misinformation 130 of 200)
estimates.denominator: 200 YouTube videos: the 100 most-viewed for appendicitis (search terms appendectomy, appendicitis, appendix surgery) and the 100 most-viewed for cholecystitis (cholecystectomy, cholecystitis, gallbladder surgery)
estimates.definition: The video scored above the lowest point ('no misinformation') on a 1-to-5 reviewer-rated misinformation scale, i.e. some, moderate, a lot or majority misinformation; examples given include inaccurate alternative treatments, home remedies for appendicitis, false recovery expectations and product promotion built on them
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given; the instrument is described as 'A Likert scale from 1 to 5 ... to estimate the amount of ... misinformation. This scale was based on the reviewer's perception of total patient education and misinformation.'
estimates.source_quote: More than a third (35%) of videos contained misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results; Table 2 (Misinformation scale: no misinformation 130 (65%), some 43 (21.5%), moderate 12 (6%), a lot 8 (4%), majority 7 (3.5%))
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four surgical trainees rated every video; on a random 10% of videos the percent agreement among the four reviewers across all items was 85%. No kappa or other chance-corrected statistic, no external standard, no rubric for the misinformation scale, and no stated adjudication rule for disagreements.
estimates.moderator_quote: YouTube was searched with keywords "cholecystectomy," "cholecystitis," and "gallbladder surgery" and "appendectomy," "appendicitis," and "appendix surgery." For each procedure, the 100 videos with the greatest views were reviewed.
estimates.notes: Denominator is rank-truncated: the 100 most-viewed videos per procedure, not a random sample of the topic, hence denom_selection curated. The misinformation label is a reviewer perception rating with no external ground truth, which weakens comparability with fact-check-anchored estimates even though it is an explicit falsity judgement. Country coded Global: no geographic restriction is placed on the videos and publisher nationality is never reported. Year 2022 is inferred (search date unreported; instrument sites accessed 9 August 2022, manuscript received 1 September 2022); the videos themselves date from a median of 2016. The 35% is stated verbatim in the abstract, so it is not a cross-category sum computed by the extractor.

estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given; the instrument is described as 'A Likert scale from 1 to 5 ... to estimate the amount of ... misinformation. This scale was based on the reviewer's perception of total patient education and misinformation.'
estimates.source_quote: Sixty five percent of videos did not contain misin- formation, while 21.5% of videos contained some misinfor- mation and 13.5% of videos contained more significant misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same four surgical trainees and same 1-to-5 misinformation scale as the broader row; 85% percent agreement among the four reviewers on a random 10% of videos across all items; no chance-corrected statistic.

estimates.notes: Stricter-threshold variant of the 35% row on the same 200 videos: do not pool both. The 13.5% is stated verbatim and matches Table 2 (moderate 6% + a lot 4% + majority 3.5%). The boundary between 'some' and 'more significant' misinformation is not defined anywhere in the paper, so what the stricter threshold means substantively is unclear.

missed_or_uncertain: Considered and not extracted: (1) The search-term split, a headline finding: '45.3% of videos discoverable using colloquial search terms contained misinformation, whereas only 20.5% of videos only discoverable using medical search terms contained misinformation (P < 0.001)', with per-procedure figures (cholecystectomy 52.2% vs 18.2%, P = 0.008; appendectomy 36% vs 22%, P = 0.123). Both values are verbatim, but the group denominators are never stated. They are recoverable from Table 1 (appendix surgery 50 + gallbladder surgery 67 = 117 colloquial-discoverable, leaving 83 medical-only; 45.3% of 117 and 20.5% of 83 sum to the 70 misinformation videos), which is a consistency check rather than a reported denominator. Not extracted because the split is by retrieval route within the same 200 videos, not by country, platform or measure, so INSTRUCTIONS §2 does not license a new row; and pooling them alongside the 35% would double-count. (2) The ten publisher-type misinformation rates in Table 3 (patient 22/28 = 78.6%, wellness channel 11/16 = 68.8%, industry 4/8 = 50%, news outlet 4/9 = 44.4%, other or unknown 9/19 = 42.1%, advocacy 1/4 = 25%, physician 13/53 = 24.5%, healthcare organization 5/26 = 19.2%, medical education 2/34 = 5.9%, academic journal 0/3 = 0%) — source subgroups of the same 200 videos; extracting ten rows would breach R4, and each is a subgroup rather than a study-level estimate. Note Table 3's publisher n values (3, 8, 28, 53, 4, 16, 26, 34, 9, 19) sum to 200 but do not match Table 1's publisher counts (advocacy is absent from Table 1 and other/unknown is 17 there, 19 in Table 3). (3) QUALITY measures, not falsity: median DISCERN 28.0 of 75; DISCERN quality bands 61.5% poor, 27% fair, 8% good, 1.5% very good, 2% excellent; median PEMAT understandability 66.7 and actionability 0; the patient-education scale distribution (49% no education, 28.5% some, 12% moderate, 4% a lot, 6.5% mostly all education) and the abstract's '22% provided moderate or more'. (4) Video and audience descriptors (62.5% general public, 22.5% patients, 40.5% healthcare providers; 23% discussed benefits, 6.5% risks, 7% alternatives, 21.5% recovery; content-type and topic counts). (5) The patient survey: '92% of patients reported using some form of social media to learn about their disease and surgery', 76% preoperatively, 52% postoperatively — social media use for health information, not exposure to misinformation, so out of scope; the survey n is also inconsistent (text says 25 patients interviewed, 13 appendectomy and 12 cholecystectomy, while Table 4 reports 20 patients, 10 and 10, with 90% referencing social media before surgery). (6) Figures cited from other studies (56% of Italian colorectal patients using the internet; 'more than half' of gallbladder videos misleading in Lee et al) — barred by R8. rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis plus a small postoperative patient survey; IRB exempt. Frame: six search terms across two conditions; videos sorted by total views and the top 100 per procedure retained, explicitly to avoid personalisation bias, giving 200 videos (median 244,815 views, median length 6:20, median publication year 2016). Search date not reported. Each video rated by four surgical trainees on DISCERN (15 items, 75 points), PEMAT (19 understandability, 4 actionability items) and two purpose-built 1-to-5 Likert scales for patient education and misinformation; the misinformation scale is explicitly perception-based with no rubric or external reference. Reliability: percent agreement of 85% among the four reviewers on a random 10% of videos across all items, with no chance-corrected statistic and no stated rule for resolving disagreement or combining the four ratings into one value per video. Analysis in SPSS 27 (Kruskal-Wallis, Pearson chi-square, alpha .05). Authors' own limitations: most-viewed videos were not necessarily made for patient education, intended audience was inferred by reviewers, only one platform was studied, and only 25 patients were surveyed.
